slides.title: Measuring what matters in development
body: Development is more than wealth. [[A country can be income-rich yet score poorly on health and education.]] Geographers therefore use composite measures that combine several dimensions of wellbeing into a single comparable figure.

The **Human Development Index** blends income, schooling and life expectancy. ==Composite indices== smooth out the distortion that a single metric like GDP can create, but they also hide internal inequality. [[A national average tells you nothing about the gap between its richest and poorest regions.]]
Better data has changed the conversation. Where once a nation was simply labelled 'developed' or 'developing', analysts now map a continuous spectrum and track movement along it year by year.

sidebar.label: Insight
sidebar.heading: Averages deceive
sidebar.quote: Two countries with identical HDI scores can feel like entirely different places to live.

slides.title: Key terms for development geography
slides.hint: Hover a highlighted key term for its definition.
body: Geographers describe inequality using a shared vocabulary. The ==Gini coefficient== captures how evenly income is spread, while the ==poverty line== marks the income below which basic needs cannot be met. [[Both measures depend on reliable national survey data, which many low-income countries lack.]]
When you compare two places, always ask what the headline figure conceals. A high average ==life expectancy== can mask sharp differences between urban and rural populations.

summary.title: In this clip
summary.body: An overview of how the Human Development Index is built and why it reframed the way nations measure progress.

paragraphs: Development used to be measured almost entirely by income. The trouble is that money alone tells you little about how long people live or whether they can read.
The Human Development Index combines three dimensions — a long and healthy life, knowledge, and a decent standard of living — into one figure between zero and one.
Because it is a composite, the HDI lets us rank and track countries, but it still averages over the inequalities inside each nation.

slides.title: Explain one limitation of the HDI
slides.question: **Explain** one limitation of using the Human Development Index to compare quality of life between countries.

stimulus.label: Recall
stimulus.text: The HDI is a national average combining income, schooling and life expectancy.

slides.model: One limitation is that the HDI is a **national average** and therefore hides inequality within a country. Two nations may share an identical HDI while one distributes wellbeing evenly and the other concentrates it in a wealthy minority, so the index alone can misrepresent how most people actually live.
criteria: Explains why it matters with reasoning

slides.title: Assess the usefulness of composite indices
slides.question: **Assess** the usefulness of composite indices for measuring development. Refer to specific examples in your answer.

stimulus.label: Stimulus
stimulus.text: Composite indices such as the HDI combine several indicators into one comparable score.

slides.scaffoldLabel: Build your response paragraph by paragraph

paragraphs.label: Introduction
paragraphs.guide: State your judgement and define a composite index.
paragraphs.model: Composite indices are **highly useful** for comparison but limited as a complete picture; this response argues they are best used alongside disaggregated data.

paragraphs.label: Strengths
paragraphs.guide: Give one strength with an example.
paragraphs.model: Their main strength is comparability: by blending health, education and income the HDI lets us rank diverse nations on a single scale and track change over time.

paragraphs.label: Limitations
paragraphs.guide: Give one limitation with an example.
paragraphs.model: However, averaging conceals inequality — a high HDI can coexist with deep regional poverty, as within rapidly urbanising states.

paragraphs.label: Judgement
paragraphs.model: On balance, composite indices are useful starting points whose conclusions must be tested against finer-grained evidence.

slides.title: Interpreting a development cartoon

source.label: Source A — political cartoon, 2019
source.transcript: A figure labelled 'Global Average' balances on a seesaw above two unequal crowds.

slides.intro: Work through each task in order, writing a response before revealing the model answer.

tasks.question: Identify the message of the source.
tasks.model: The source argues that a single global average disguises a deeply unequal reality beneath it.

tasks.question: Explain how the cartoonist conveys this message.
tasks.model: By placing the 'average' figure on a seesaw above two unequal crowds, the cartoonist visually equates an average with an unstable balancing act that ignores the spread below.

tasks.question: Assess the usefulness of this source for a geographer studying inequality.
tasks.model: It is useful for prompting critical thinking about averages, though as opinion it offers no data and would need pairing with statistical evidence.
